title: Deep Learning · Chapter 2
description: Deep neural networks: supervised learning, notation, 1D linear regression and loss, generalisation, shallow neural networks, parameter counting and training with backpropagation.

topics.title: Supervised Learning
topics.description: Labelled data, mapping inputs to outputs, models and parameters, classification vs regression, problem types, Figures A and B.

questions.prompt: What is supervised learning?

image.alt: Diagram of supervised learning: labelled training data is used to train a model that predicts labels for new data.

options.text: A type of ML where a model learns from labelled data — every input has a corresponding correct output
Learning from unlabelled data by finding clusters
Learning by trial and error with rewards

questions.explanation: Labelled data = input plus its correct answer.

questions.prompt: In supervised learning, what does the algorithm learn?

options.text: A mapping function from input (X) to output (Y)
How to group data without labels
A mapping from output to input

questions.explanation: It observes examples where the correct answer is provided.

questions.prompt: What does a supervised learning model do during training? (select all that apply)

options.text: Compares predictions with the true outputs

questions.explanation: Predict → compare → adjust, improving accuracy over time.

questions.prompt: What is the GOAL of a supervised learning model?

options.text: To make accurate predictions on new, unseen data
To use as few parameters as possible
To memorise the training data perfectly

questions.explanation: E.g. a model trained on handwritten digits recognises new digits it has never seen.

questions.prompt: Which order shows the supervised-learning mapping?

options.text: Model input → real-world input → model → real-world output → model output
Real-world output → model output → model → model input → real-world input
Real-world input → model input → model → model output → real-world output
Model → real-world input → model output → model input → real-world output

questions.explanation: A real-world thing is encoded as a model input, the model maps it, and the model output is decoded into a real-world answer.

questions.prompt: Mathematically, what is a supervised learning model?

options.text: A table of all possible answers
A mapping (a mathematical equation) from one or more inputs to one or more outputs

questions.explanation: The model is an equation; training picks which equation fits best.

questions.prompt: What is INFERENCE?

options.text: Running the trained model on an input to compute its output (prediction)
Computing the inputs from the outputs

questions.explanation: Inference = using the model: input in, output out. ⚠️ Your notes say “computing the inputs from the outputs” — that's back to front. Inference computes the OUTPUTS from the INPUTS.

questions.prompt: What do a model's PARAMETERS do?

options.text: They affect the outcome of the equation — so one model represents a whole family of equations
They are the inputs to the model

questions.explanation: Changing parameters picks a different equation from the family.

questions.prompt: What does “training a model” mean?

options.text: Running the model on new data
Writing the model's equation by hand
Finding parameters that predict outputs well from inputs, for a training dataset of input/output pairs

questions.explanation: Training = searching for good parameter values.

questions.prompt: In the simple model that predicts a child's height from age, what is x?

image.alt: Simple model: x (model input, age of child) goes into y = f(x) (supervised learning model), producing y (model output, height of child).

options.text: The model input — the child's age
The model output — the child's height

questions.explanation: x (age) → y = f[x] → y (height).

questions.prompt: The model gives y = 139 cm for x = 10 years. What is 139 cm here?

image.alt: Model example: input x is 10 years, the model graph maps it, and the output is y = 139 cm.

options.text: The training label for every child
The model output — the predicted height

questions.explanation: The model is an equation relating input (age) to output (height).

questions.prompt: Fitting deep neural networks to data is what we call “deep learning”.
questions.explanation: Deep neural networks are just a very flexible family of equations, and fitting them = deep learning.

questions.prompt: What are the two types of supervised learning? (select all that apply)

image.alt: Mind map: supervised learning splits into classification and regression.

questions.explanation: Clustering is unsupervised; reinforcement is its own type.

questions.prompt: When the output is a CATEGORICAL variable (e.g. spam vs not spam), the task is…
questions.explanation: Discrete classes → classification.

questions.prompt: When the output is a CONTINUOUS variable (e.g. house price), the task is…
questions.explanation: Continuous numbers → regression.

questions.prompt: Predicting tomorrow's stock price is…
questions.explanation: A continuous number.

questions.prompt: In Figure A (shopping store dataset), what is the OUTPUT?

image.alt: Figure A: shopping store dataset with columns for gender, age, salary and purchased (0 or 1).

questions.explanation: Inputs are gender, age and salary; the output is a 0/1 class, so this is classification.

questions.prompt: What kind of supervised learning problem is Figure A?
questions.explanation: The output has two discrete classes (0 or 1).

questions.prompt: In Figure B (meteorological dataset), which are INPUTS? (select all that apply)

image.alt: Figure B: meteorological dataset with dew point, temperature, pressure, relative humidity, wind direction and wind speed columns.

questions.explanation: Wind speed is the output.

questions.prompt: Figure B predicts wind speed. What kind of problem is it?

options.text: Regression — the output is a continuous number

questions.explanation: Wind speed is a real value.

questions.prompt: Predicting ONE real-valued output (e.g. one price) is a…

image.alt: Univariate regression example: one real-valued output predicted by a fully connected deep neural network.

questions.explanation: Univariate = one output.

questions.prompt: Predicting MORE THAN ONE real-valued output is a…

image.alt: Graph regression example: more than one real-valued output predicted by a graph neural network.

questions.explanation: Multivariate = >1 output.

questions.prompt: Classifying text into two classes (e.g. positive / negative) is a…

image.alt: Text classification example: text is classified into one of two classes by a transformer network.

questions.explanation: Two discrete classes.

questions.prompt: Classifying music into one of many genres is a…

image.alt: Music genre classification example: audio is classified into one of several genres by a recurrent neural network.

questions.explanation: More than two discrete classes.

questions.prompt: In your notes, which network type is used for IMAGE classification?

image.alt: Image classification example: a picture is classified into one of several classes by a convolutional neural network.

questions.explanation: Image → CNN; music genre → RNN; text → Transformer; graph regression → GNN; univariate regression → fully connected DNN.

questions.prompt: In your notes, which network type is paired with MUSIC GENRE classification?
questions.explanation: RNNs handle sequences such as audio over time.

questions.prompt: In your notes, which network type is paired with TEXT classification?
questions.explanation: Transformers power modern NLP.

questions.prompt: In your notes, which network type is paired with the multivariate GRAPH regression example?
questions.explanation: Graph inputs → GNN.

topics.title: Supervised Learning Steps, Terms & Notation
topics.description: The 5 key steps (CSTVD), the 80/20 split, important terms and the notation for inputs, models, loss, training and testing.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the key supervised learning steps (CSTVD)?

options.text: Collect labelled data → Split the dataset → Train → Validate & test → Deploy & predict

questions.explanation: CSTVD.

questions.prompt: When splitting the dataset, roughly what percentage is used for TRAINING?
questions.explanation: About 80% training, 20% testing.

questions.prompt: Why is the model evaluated on testing data it has never seen before?

options.text: To check how well it generalises to new data
Because training data is too small

questions.explanation: Predictions on the test set are compared with the true labels to calculate accuracy or error.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms are named in your notes for the training step? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: K-means is unsupervised clustering.

questions.prompt: In step 1, “images of handwritten digits with their actual numbers” is an example of…
questions.explanation: Each image has its correct label.

questions.prompt: Match the terms — which are correct? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Univariate/multivariate refer to the number of OUTPUTS here.

questions.prompt: Two-class and multiclass classification are treated differently.
questions.explanation: E.g. sigmoid + binary cross-entropy for two classes, softmax + categorical cross-entropy for many.

questions.prompt: In the notation, variables (inputs x, outputs y) are always written with…
questions.explanation: Variables = Roman letters; parameters = Greek letters.

questions.prompt: Parameters are always written with…
questions.explanation: e.g. φ (phi) for parameters.

questions.prompt: Which Greek letter is used for the model's parameters in y = f[x, φ]? (name it)
questions.explanation: φ = phi.

questions.prompt: In the notation, a BOLD lowercase letter (e.g. 𝐱) means…
questions.explanation: Normal = scalar, bold = vector, capital bold = matrix.

questions.prompt: A CAPITAL BOLD letter (e.g. 𝐗) means…
questions.explanation: Capital bold = matrix.

questions.prompt: Functions are always written with which brackets?
questions.explanation: e.g. y = f[x, φ].

questions.prompt: What does the loss (cost) function measure?

options.text: How many layers the network has
How many parameters the model has
How bad the model is — a scalar that is smaller when the model maps inputs to outputs better

questions.explanation: Lower loss = better fit.

questions.prompt: What does this notation describe?

options.text: A training dataset of I pairs of input/output examples

questions.explanation: {xᵢ, yᵢ} for i = 1 … I.

questions.prompt: What does this equation mean?

options.text: The loss is set to φ
The best parameters φ̂ are the ones that minimise the loss L[φ]

questions.explanation: Training = find the parameters that minimise the loss.

questions.prompt: How is a model TESTED?

options.text: Run it on a separate test dataset of input/output pairs to see how well it generalises
Run it again on the training data

questions.explanation: Testing measures generalisation to new data.

topics.title: 1D Linear Regression, Loss & Generalisation
topics.description: y = φ₀ + φ₁x, least-squares loss, gradient descent, testing, underfitting and overfitting.

questions.prompt: In the 1D linear regression model below, what is φ₀?
questions.explanation: φ₀ = y-offset, φ₁ = slope.

questions.prompt: In the same model, what is φ₁?
questions.explanation: φ₁ controls how steep the line is.

questions.prompt: The model y = φ₀ + φ₁x represents…

options.text: A family of all possible straight lines

questions.explanation: Each choice of φ₀, φ₁ gives a different line.

questions.prompt: Which line in the graph is φ₀ = 0.0, φ₁ = 1.0?

image.alt: Graph of output y against input x from 0 to 2 with three straight lines: A rises from (0,0) to (2,2); B is almost flat, starting at 1.2 and falling slightly to 1.0; C starts at 1.0 and falls to 0.2.

questions.explanation: It starts at 0 (offset 0) and rises 1 unit per unit of x.

questions.prompt: Which line in the graph is φ₀ = 1.0, φ₁ = −0.4?

image.alt: Graph of output y against input x from 0 to 2 with three straight lines: A rises from (0,0) to (2,2); B is almost flat, starting at 1.2 and falling slightly to 1.0; C starts at 1.0 and falls to 0.2.

questions.explanation: Starts at y = 1.0 and falls 0.4 per unit of x (to 0.2 at x = 2). Line B is φ₀ = 1.2, φ₁ = −0.1.

questions.prompt: For φ₀ = 1.0 and φ₁ = −0.4, what is y when x = 1.5?
What is the name of this loss function?
questions.code:
L[φ] = Σᵢ ( f[xᵢ, φ] − yᵢ )²
     = Σᵢ ( φ₀ + φ₁xᵢ − yᵢ )²
questions.explanation: It sums the squared differences between predictions and true outputs.

questions.prompt: Two training points: (x=1, y=2) and (x=2, y=3). With φ₀ = 0.5 and φ₁ = 1, what is the least squares loss?
questions.explanation: Predictions 1.5 and 2.5 → errors −0.5 and −0.5 → 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: Three candidate lines are fitted to the same data. Which has the SMALLEST least squares loss?

image.alt: Scatter of 12 training points with the line φ₀ = 1.60, φ₁ = -0.80 and dashed red lines showing each point's error.
Scatter of 12 training points with the line φ₀ = 0.84, φ₁ = 0.50 and dashed red lines showing each point's error.
Scatter of 12 training points with the line φ₀ = 0.40, φ₁ = 0.20 and dashed red lines showing each point's error.

questions.explanation: Shorter dashed error lines → smaller squared errors. With this data the losses are about 6.70, 10.96 and 0.21.

questions.prompt: Why are the errors SQUARED in least squares loss?

options.text: So positive and negative errors don't cancel out, and big errors are penalised more
It's only a convention with no effect

questions.explanation: Squaring makes every error positive and punishes large mistakes.

questions.prompt: How do we find a GOOD model?

options.text: Find the best parameters — the ones that minimise the loss
Add more data until loss is zero
Pick the line that passes through the first point

questions.explanation: φ̂ = argmin L[φ].

questions.prompt: This picture shows the loss for every intercept/slope pair, with steps moving downhill to the lowest loss. What is this technique called?

image.alt: Contour plot of loss with intercept φ₀ on the horizontal axis and slope φ₁ on the vertical axis. Red dots step from a start point near (1.6, −0.8) down to the lowest-loss point near (0.8, 0.5).

questions.explanation: Gradient descent repeatedly steps in the direction that reduces the loss.

questions.prompt: The loss can be drawn as a contour graph with intercept and slope on the axes.
questions.explanation: Each point on the contour is one possible line; the lowest point is the best line.

questions.prompt: Why test with a SEPARATE, unseen set of input/output pairs?

options.text: To increase the number of parameters
Because training data has no labels
To measure performance on new data (generalisation)

questions.explanation: The degree to which test performance matches training performance is generalisation.

questions.prompt: A model that is TOO SIMPLE and doesn't even fit the training data well is…
questions.explanation: Too simple → underfitting.

questions.prompt: A model that is TOO COMPLEX and fits the statistical peculiarities (noise) of the training data is…
questions.explanation: Too complex → overfitting.

questions.prompt: Which fit shows OVERFITTING?

image.alt: A straight line through wavy data points, missing the curve.
A smooth curve that follows the overall wave of the data points.
A wiggly curve passing through every data point and shooting off at the edges.

questions.explanation: The wiggly curve hits every training point but would predict new data badly.

questions.prompt: Which fit GENERALISES best?

image.alt: A wiggly curve passing through every data point and shooting off at the edges.
A smooth curve that follows the overall wave of the data points.
A straight line through wavy data points, missing the curve.

questions.explanation: The smooth curve captures the real pattern without chasing the noise.

questions.prompt: This straight line through curved data is an example of…

image.alt: A straight line through wavy data points, missing the curve.

questions.explanation: The model is too simple to capture the curve.

topics.title: Shallow Neural Networks: Architecture
topics.description: Components (input, hidden, output, node), what each layer does, neurons, and choosing the output activation.

questions.prompt: What are the components of a neural network (IHON)? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: IHON.

questions.prompt: Where does the network learn the relationships and interactions between the input variables?
questions.explanation: Hidden layers sit between input and output.

questions.prompt: What is a node (neuron)?

options.text: A computational unit that takes one or more input values and produces an output value

questions.explanation: Nodes are the circles in network diagrams.

questions.prompt: In this artificial neuron, what usually goes in the box marked “?” after the weighted sum?

image.alt: Artificial neuron: inputs x₁, x₂, x₃ multiplied by weights w₁, w₂, w₃ flow into a Σ circle labelled plus bias b, producing z, which goes into a box marked with a question mark and a[z], then to the output.

options.text: An activation function a[z] (e.g. ReLU, sigmoid)

questions.explanation: Inputs × weights, summed with a bias (z), then passed through an activation function to give the output.

questions.prompt: What is a SHALLOW neural network?

options.text: A neural network with a small number of layers — often just one hidden layer
A network with more than 100 layers
A network with no hidden layers and no output
A network that only works on images

questions.explanation: One hidden layer = shallow; more than one = deep.

questions.prompt: Shallow neural networks are typically used for…

options.text: Simple tasks such as regression or classification

questions.explanation: Simple regression and classification.

questions.prompt: In this example network, what are x₁ and x₂?

image.alt: Shallow network: inputs x₁ and x₂ connect to hidden nodes n₁ and n₂, which connect to one output y.

options.text: Input variables fed into the hidden nodes n₁ and n₂

questions.explanation: x₁ and x₂ feed into the two nodes of the single hidden layer, which then generate the output. (Your notes call them “response variables”, but they are the INPUT variables — the response is the output.)

questions.prompt: What does the INPUT layer do? (select all that apply)

options.text: Has one neuron per input feature

questions.explanation: Computation starts in the hidden layer.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 4 features. How many neurons are in the input layer?
questions.explanation: Number of input neurons = number of features.

questions.prompt: What does each HIDDEN neuron do? (select all that apply)

options.text: Computes a weighted sum of the previous layer's outputs

questions.explanation: Weighted sum + bias → activation.

questions.prompt: Why do hidden layers use activation functions like ReLU, Sigmoid or Tanh?

options.text: They introduce non-linearity so the network can learn complex, non-linear relationships

questions.explanation: Without non-linearity, stacked layers would just be one straight-line model.

questions.prompt: How many output neurons for a 5-class classification task?
questions.explanation: K classes → K output neurons (with softmax).

questions.prompt: How many output neurons for binary classification or regression?
questions.explanation: One neuron for binary classification or a single regression value.

questions.prompt: Which output activation is used for BINARY classification?
questions.explanation: Sigmoid squashes to 0–1, a probability.

questions.prompt: Which output activation is used for MULTI-CLASS classification?
questions.explanation: Softmax turns K scores into K probabilities that add to 1.

questions.prompt: In this decision tree, which output activation goes in the “?” box for regression?

image.alt: Decision tree: task splits into regression (output activation marked ?) and classification; classification with 2 classes uses sigmoid with 1 neuron, more than 2 classes uses softmax with K neurons.

questions.explanation: Regression outputs any real number, so the output layer uses a linear function.

topics.title: How a Shallow Network Computes
topics.description: Weighted sum → activation → output, ReLU, weights and biases, activations, piecewise linear functions and the universal approximation theorem.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of how a shallow network works (WAO)?

options.text: Weighted sum → Activation function → Output generation

questions.explanation: WAO.

questions.prompt: What is the graph's function a[z]?

image.alt: Graph of an activation function: flat at zero for negative z, then rising in a straight line with slope 1 for positive z.

options.text: ReLU: 0 when z < 0, z when z ≥ 0

questions.explanation: ReLU = Rectified Linear Unit: flat at zero for negative inputs, then a straight line.

questions.prompt: What does ReLU stand for?
questions.explanation: ReLU = Rectified Linear Unit.

questions.prompt: What is ReLU[−3]?
questions.explanation: Negative inputs become 0.

questions.prompt: What is ReLU[2.5]?
questions.explanation: Non-negative inputs pass through unchanged.

questions.prompt: In a shallow network, which statements are correct? (select all that apply)

image.alt: Shallow network with one input x, three hidden units h₁, h₂, h₃ and one output y. Edges into the hidden units are labelled θ₁₁, θ₂₁, θ₃₁ with biases θ₁₀, θ₂₀, θ₃₀; edges to the output are labelled φ₁, φ₂, φ₃ with bias φ₀.

questions.explanation: Weights = slopes, biases = offsets, pre-activations go into ReLU, activations come out.

questions.prompt: Network parameters are…
questions.explanation: Total parameters = all weights + all biases.

questions.prompt: One hidden layer = shallow neural network. More than one hidden layer = …
questions.explanation: Deep = multiple hidden layers.

questions.prompt: In these equations, what is h₁?
questions.code:
h₁ = a[θ₁₀ + θ₁₁x]
h₂ = a[θ₂₀ + θ₂₁x]
h₃ = a[θ₃₀ + θ₃₁x]

y  = φ₀ + φ₁h₁ + φ₂h₂ + φ₃h₃

options.text: A hidden unit — the activation of the first hidden neuron

questions.explanation: h = hidden unit = a[pre-activation].

questions.prompt: θ₁₀ = −0.4, θ₁₁ = 1.0 and x = 1.2. What is h₁ = ReLU[θ₁₀ + θ₁₁x]?
questions.explanation: Pre-activation = −0.4 + 1.0 × 1.2 = 0.8; ReLU keeps it: 0.8.

questions.prompt: Using the parameters below, what is y when x = 2?
questions.code:
θ₁₀ = 1,   θ₁₁ = −1
θ₂₀ = −1,  θ₂₁ = 1
θ₃₀ = 0.5, θ₃₁ = 0.5

φ₀ = 0.5,  φ₁ = 2
φ₂ = 1,    φ₃ = −1

questions.prompt: What is the correct order to build the output of a 3-hidden-unit network?

options.text: Compute three linear functions → pass through ReLU → weight the hidden units → sum them (+ φ₀)
Sum → ReLU → weight → compute linear functions
Weight the hidden units → compute linear functions → ReLU → sum
Pass through ReLU → compute linear functions → sum → weight

questions.explanation: 1) θ linear functions, 2) ReLU creates hidden units, 3) multiply by φ, 4) add together with φ₀.

questions.prompt: Which panel shows the hidden units AFTER passing through ReLU (negative parts clipped to zero)?

image.alt: Four panels labelled a to d. a: three straight lines. b: the same lines with negative parts flattened to zero. c: the flattened lines scaled up, down or flipped. d: one purple line made of straight pieces with three joints circled.

questions.explanation: a = linear functions, b = after ReLU, c = weighted by φ, d = sum + φ₀.

questions.prompt: Which panel shows the final network OUTPUT?

image.alt: Four panels labelled a to d. a: three straight lines. b: the same lines with negative parts flattened to zero. c: the flattened lines scaled up, down or flipped. d: one purple line made of straight pieces with three joints circled.

questions.explanation: The sum of the weighted hidden units plus φ₀ is a piecewise linear function.

questions.prompt: What kind of function does a shallow ReLU network with one input produce?

options.text: A piecewise linear function — straight pieces joined at “joints”

questions.explanation: Each ReLU adds one joint.

questions.prompt: This network output has 3 joints. How many ReLU hidden units created them (at least)?

image.alt: Output y against input x: a line made of four straight pieces joined at three circled joints.

questions.explanation: 1 joint per ReLU function.

questions.prompt: A shallow network has D = 10 ReLU hidden units and one input. At most how many joints can its output have?
questions.explanation: Up to one joint per hidden unit → up to 10 joints (11 linear regions).

questions.prompt: What does the universal approximation theorem say?

image.alt: A wavy grey target function closely followed by a purple line made of many straight segments (11 joints).

options.text: Any network always gives zero loss
With enough hidden units, a shallow network can describe any continuous function (on a compact subset of ℝᴰ) to arbitrary precision
A network with one hidden unit can fit any data

questions.explanation: More hidden units → more joints → closer approximation.

questions.prompt: For D hidden units, which pair of equations is correct?

options.text: h_d = a[x]   and   y = φ₀·Σ h_d
h_d = a[θ_d0 + θ_d1·x]   and   y = φ₀ + Σ φ_d·h_d
h_d = θ_d0 + θ_d1·x   and   y = a[Σ h_d]

questions.explanation: Same form as 3 hidden units, summed from d = 1 to D.

topics.title: Multiple Inputs/Outputs & Counting Parameters
topics.description: Networks with several inputs or outputs, the general case, and the parameter-counting exercises from your notes.

questions.prompt: How many parameters does this network (1 input, 3 hidden units, 1 output) have?

image.alt: Shallow network with one input x, three hidden units h₁, h₂, h₃ and one output y. Edges into the hidden units are labelled θ₁₁, θ₂₁, θ₃₁ with biases θ₁₀, θ₂₀, θ₃₀; edges to the output are labelled φ₁, φ₂, φ₃ with bias φ₀.

questions.explanation: Hidden: 3 weights + 3 biases = 6. Output: 3 weights + 1 bias = 4. Total = 10.

questions.prompt: Exercise from your notes: 1 input, 6 hidden units, 1 output. How many parameters?

image.alt: Shallow network: one input x, six hidden units h₁ to h₆, one output y.

questions.explanation: Hidden: 6 weights + 6 biases = 12. Output: 6 weights + 1 bias = 7. Total = 19.

questions.prompt: 1 input, 4 hidden units, 2 outputs. How many parameters?

image.alt: Shallow network: one input x, four hidden units, two outputs y₁ and y₂.

questions.explanation: Hidden: 4 + 4 = 8. Outputs: each has 4 weights + 1 bias = 5, × 2 = 10. Total = 18.

questions.prompt: 2 inputs, 3 hidden units, 1 output. How many parameters?

image.alt: Shallow network: two inputs x₁ and x₂, three hidden units, one output y.

questions.explanation: Hidden: each unit has 2 weights + 1 bias = 3, × 3 = 9. Output: 3 weights + 1 bias = 4. Total = 13.

questions.prompt: From your notes: 3 inputs, 3 hidden units, 2 outputs. How many parameters?

image.alt: Shallow network: three inputs, three hidden units, two outputs.

questions.explanation: Hidden: 3 × (3 weights + 1 bias) = 12. Outputs: 2 × (3 weights + 1 bias) = 8. Total = 20.

questions.prompt: In general, with Dᵢ inputs, D hidden units and Dₒ outputs, how many parameters are there?
questions.explanation: Each hidden unit: Dᵢ weights + 1 bias. Each output: D weights + 1 bias.

questions.prompt: With 2 inputs, what is the hidden unit h₁?
questions.explanation: Each hidden unit takes a weighted sum of ALL inputs plus its bias.

questions.prompt: With 2 outputs, how is y₂ computed?

options.text: y₂ = φ₂₀ + φ₂₁h₁ + φ₂₂h₂ + φ₂₃h₃ + φ₂₄h₄

questions.explanation: Each output has its own bias and its own weight for every hidden unit.

questions.prompt: Spam detector exercise: 3 input features (keyword, sender domain, attachments), 5 hidden units. Which design choices are right? (select all that apply)

image.alt: Spam detector network: 3 inputs (keyword, domain, attachments), 5 hidden ReLU units, 1 sigmoid output.

options.text: 1 output neuron with a sigmoid activation
Mean squared error as the loss

questions.explanation: Spam / not spam is binary classification → 1 sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy loss.

questions.prompt: How many parameters does the spam detector (3 inputs, 5 hidden units, 1 output) have?
questions.explanation: Hidden: 5 × (3 + 1) = 20. Output: 5 + 1 = 6. Total = 26.

questions.prompt: Iris exercise: 4 features (sepal length/width, petal length/width), 5 hidden units, 3 species. Which are right? (select all that apply)

image.alt: Iris classifier network: 4 inputs, 5 hidden units, 3 softmax outputs (setosa, versicolor, virginica).

questions.explanation: 3 species = multiclass → 3 softmax outputs + categorical cross-entropy.

questions.prompt: How many parameters does the Iris network (4 inputs, 5 hidden, 3 outputs) have?

topics.title: Training: Forward Prop, Loss & Backprop
topics.description: Forward propagation, loss functions (MSE, binary and categorical cross-entropy), backpropagation, weight updates and epochs.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of training a shallow network?

options.text: Weight update → Loss calculation → Forward propagation → Backpropagation
Backpropagation → Forward propagation → Weight update → Loss calculation
Forward propagation → Loss calculation → Backpropagation → Weight update (repeat for many epochs)
Loss calculation → Weight update → Backpropagation → Forward propagation

questions.explanation: Forward pass, measure error, compute gradients backwards, update, repeat.

questions.prompt: Calculating the output for a given input by passing it through the layers is…
questions.explanation: Input → hidden → output.

questions.prompt: Calculating the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight is…
questions.explanation: It tells us how to adjust each weight to reduce the loss.

questions.prompt: What is an epoch?

options.text: One pass of the training process over the data; training repeats for many epochs until the network learns

questions.explanation: Training iterates over many epochs.

questions.prompt: What is the GOAL of training?

options.text: Minimise the loss and improve accuracy on unseen data
Use as many epochs as possible

questions.explanation: Low loss and good generalisation.

questions.prompt: In the forward pass, what is ŷ?

image.alt: Scatter of 12 true data points with a purple line of predictions ŷ and dashed red lines showing the error at each point.

questions.explanation: ŷ = prediction; y = true value.

questions.prompt: What is a loss function for? (select all that apply)

options.text: Quantifies how good or bad the model's prediction is
Gives feedback to optimisers like gradient descent

questions.explanation: Loss guides the weight updates.

questions.prompt: Which loss is used for REGRESSION (continuous values)?
questions.explanation: MSE = average of squared differences.

questions.prompt: Which loss is used for BINARY classification?
questions.explanation: Two classes → binary cross-entropy.

questions.prompt: Which loss is used for MULTICLASS classification?
questions.explanation: More than two classes.

questions.prompt: Which loss function is this?
questions.explanation: Average (1/N) of squared differences.

questions.prompt: Which loss function is this?
questions.explanation: The y and (1 − y) terms handle the two classes.

questions.prompt: In categorical cross-entropy L = −Σ yᵢ log(ŷᵢ), what is C (the number the sum goes up to)?
questions.code:
L(y, ŷ) = − Σ  yᵢ · log(ŷᵢ)
          i=1..C
questions.explanation: yᵢ = true label for class i, ŷᵢ = predicted probability for class i, C = number of classes.

questions.prompt: Using the table, what is the squared error (ŷ − y)² for x = 0.86?
Using all 12 rows, what is the MSE (approximately)?
questions.explanation: The squared errors add up to 0.228; 0.228 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.019. (Your notes say ≈ 0.018 — the slide probably used unrounded ŷ values.) 0.228 is the sum, not the mean.

questions.prompt: For one example with true label y = 1, binary cross-entropy simplifies to…
questions.explanation: When y = 1 the (1 − y) term disappears. ŷ = 0.9 gives −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105 (small loss); ŷ = 0.1 gives ≈ 2.30 (big loss).

questions.prompt: True class is the 2nd of 3 (one-hot y = [0, 1, 0]) and the model predicts ŷ = [0.2, 0.7, 0.1]. What is the categorical cross-entropy (natural log)?
questions.explanation: Only the true class's term survives because the other yᵢ are 0.

questions.prompt: Backpropagation computes gradients using…
questions.explanation: Errors are propagated layer by layer from output back to input.

questions.prompt: In which direction does backpropagation go through the network?

options.text: From the output layer back to the input

questions.explanation: Hence “back”-propagation.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the backpropagation steps?

options.text: Update parameters → Compute error gradient → Calculate partial derivatives
Calculate partial derivatives → Update parameters → Compute error gradient
Compute the error gradient → Calculate partial derivatives → Update parameters (weights & biases)

questions.explanation: Then repeat across many epochs.

questions.prompt: How are weights updated after backpropagation?

options.text: Add the gradient to each weight
Multiply each weight by the loss
Subtract a fraction of the gradient (learning rate × gradient) from each weight

questions.explanation: w_new = w_old − learning rate × ∂L/∂w — this moves downhill on the loss.

questions.prompt: A weight is 0.8, the gradient ∂L/∂w is 2 and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the new weight?
